stories.body: Iran-aligned Houthi rebels seized the strategic Yemeni Red Sea port city of Mocha and were advancing toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait, according to the Yemeni government and military sources. The fighting is part of a broader escalation across Taiz, the western coast, al-Jawf, Marib and Dhalea that aid agencies say has killed at least 194 people and wounded 880 in two weeks. Analysts say control of the heights and roads linking Taiz and Mocha could give the Houthis greater leverage near the southern entrance to the Red Sea, a crucial shipping chokepoint connecting Europe and Asia.
stories.headline: Houthi forces seize Yemen's Red Sea port of Mocha and advance toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait

stories.body: Iran and the United States exchanged their largest wave of attacks on shipping since their war began, with Iran saying it struck 10 vessels near the Strait of Hormuz after US forces sank five Iranian oil tankers. Brent crude rose above $100 a barrel on fears over global energy supplies. The jump in oil prices pushed Asian stocks lower and heightened expectations that the Federal Reserve and other central banks could raise interest rates to contain inflation.
stories.headline: Iran-US attacks on shipping drive oil above $100 and raise inflation fears

stories.body: The International Atomic Energy Agency said satellite imagery and state-media photographs show that North Korea has built a new uranium-enrichment facility at Yongbyon, its main nuclear complex, and expanded activity at Kangson near Pyongyang. The Yongbyon building could hold up to 28 centrifuge cascades; a cited analysis estimated that capacity could produce about 85 kilograms of weapons-grade uranium a year, enough for three or four additional warheads. IAEA chief Rafael Grossi called the continuing expansion a serious concern and a violation of UN Security Council resolutions.
stories.headline: UN nuclear watchdog says North Korea has built a new uranium facility

stories.body: At least five people were killed and more than 80 remained unaccounted for after the passenger ferry MV June Aster caught fire near Coron off the Philippine island province of Palawan. The vessel left Manila with 117 passengers and 17 crew, and 43 people had been rescued as coast guard teams searched with ships, drones and drift-modelling tools. Thick smoke, extreme heat, strong currents and the risk of explosions prevented rescuers from entering the vessel; preliminary survivor accounts suggest the blaze began in the cargo hold.
stories.headline: Philippines ferry fire kills at least five as search continues for dozens missing

stories.body: Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least seven people, Ukrainian officials said, including four in Mykolaiv and three in a drone strike on a shopping centre in Sumy. Meanwhile, Ukraine's Special Operations Forces said it struck two major gas-processing plants in Russia's Yamal-Nenets Arctic region, more than 3,000 kilometres from the Ukrainian border. Russian authorities said an industrial facility in Novy Urengoy caught fire after falling drone debris, while Kyiv described the operation as its deepest strike inside Russia since the full-scale invasion began.
stories.headline: Russian attacks kill seven in Ukraine as Kyiv strikes Arctic gas facilities

stories.body: President Donald Trump said he would give every adult American $5,000 if Republicans retain both chambers of Congress in November's midterm elections, without explaining how the plan would be funded or administered. With nearly 270 million adults in the country, the proposal would cost roughly $1.3 trillion. Trump and Vice President JD Vance linked the idea to tariff revenue, while critics questioned its feasibility and legality amid rising living costs and oil prices tied to the Iran war.
stories.headline: Trump promises $5,000 payments to every adult American if Republicans retain Congress

stories.body: Republicans gathering at their midterm convention in Dallas voiced private concern that high gasoline prices, the Iran war, a deepening trade dispute with Canada and broader cost-of-living pressures are damaging their electoral prospects. Oil reached $100 a barrel after new strikes against Iran, while party candidates and officials discussed how to defend vulnerable races and reclaim their economic message. Some Republicans blamed Democrats for affordability problems, but others acknowledged that campaign spending cannot offset voters' highly visible concern over fuel and household costs.
stories.headline: Republicans confront cost-of-living and oil-price pressures at their midterm convention

stories.body: Former CVS executive Helena Foulkes defeated Rhode Island Governor Dan McKee in the Democratic primary, making McKee the first sitting US governor to lose a primary since 2018. Foulkes focused her campaign on McKee's handling of the troubled Washington Bridge reconstruction, which has been marked by delays, cost overruns and disputes over accountability. The bridge was partially closed in 2023 and is now not expected to be completed until 2028.
stories.headline: Former CVS executive Helena Foulkes defeats Rhode Island Governor Dan McKee in Democratic primary

stories.body: The US Supreme Court has been asked to intervene in a Missouri dispute over a new congressional map that favors Republicans, after conflicting lower-court rulings created uncertainty over which map the state can use for November's midterm elections. The appeal seeks a resolution before election preparations are further disrupted.
stories.headline: Supreme Court is asked to resolve Missouri congressional-map dispute ahead of the midterms

stories.body: Spain's government released 40 declassified reports and communications on the mass entry of an estimated 70,000 to 80,000 people into Ceuta in late July. The documents show that the CNI intelligence service warned Moroccan authorities, the government delegation in Ceuta and the Civil Guard a day earlier about online calls for a crossing, including groups with 180,000 followers, but did not anticipate the scale of the event. The disclosures have sharpened the political dispute over whether authorities were adequately warned and whether Morocco's role was properly assessed.
stories.headline: Declassified intelligence documents intensify Spain's dispute over warnings before the Ceuta mass crossing

stories.body: Spain's Supreme Court temporarily suspended the registration of people who acquired Spanish nationality through the Democratic Memory Law, known as the descendants' law, in the overseas electoral register unless they can prove descent from Spaniards exiled by the Civil War or Franco dictatorship. The ruling does not halt nationality grants, but prevents affected people from voting while the case proceeds. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez criticized the decision and urged a swift resolution, accusing the right of joining a broader far-right effort to cast doubt on democratic processes.
stories.headline: Spain's Supreme Court suspension of voting rights under the descendants' law sparks political clash

stories.body: Spain's Congress is set to vote on a law that would grant Spanish nationality to Sahrawis born under Spanish administration in Western Sahara and their descendants, potentially affecting up to 200,000 people in the territory, Algerian refugee camps and the European diaspora. Supporters describe it as historical redress, while the debate has become entangled with Spain's migration tensions with Morocco and criticism of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's 2022 shift toward Morocco's position on Western Sahara. Most parliamentary groups backed the measure but used the debate to demand a reversal of that policy change.
stories.headline: Spanish Congress prepares to vote on citizenship for Sahrawis born under Spanish rule and their descendants

stories.body: Josep Lluís Trapero resigned as director general of Catalonia's police after two years in the role, amid tensions within the Interior Department and the Mossos d'Esquadra leadership. Interior Minister Núria Parlon said the decision was personal and praised his work, while reporting points to disagreements over senior appointments, including the replacement of the department's second-ranking official and a change in Mossos police leadership. Ferran López Navarro will replace Trapero, and Sílvia Catà Culubret will become the new chief commissioner of the Mossos.
stories.headline: Catalonia's police director Josep Lluís Trapero resigns amid leadership tensions

stories.body: Catalonia recorded 556 deaths by suicide or self-harm in 2025, provisional national statistics show, a 17% decline in the mortality rate since 2022 but still a major public-health concern. Men accounted for 413 deaths and women for 143. Separately, Barcelona reported rising suicidal thoughts and attempts since 2021, particularly among young people, even as suicide deaths have been relatively stable; the city has launched a 2026-32 prevention strategy including risk mapping, professional training and an eviction-intervention protocol.
stories.headline: Catalonia records 556 deaths by suicide or self-harm in 2025 despite a three-year decline

stories.body: Metges de Catalunya has announced an indefinite strike beginning in mid-October, with the precise date still to be agreed, alongside a new national confederation of seven medical unions. The unions oppose the government's proposed reform of the health-service employment framework, which they say preserves unfair and discriminatory conditions for doctors. They are seeking a separate regulatory framework recognizing doctors' distinct responsibilities, training and working conditions, and the Catalan union is also demanding negotiations with the regional Health Department.
stories.headline: Catalan doctors announce an indefinite strike beginning in October

stories.body: Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni reaffirmed that the city's roughly 10,000 tourist-flat licences will disappear in 2028, saying a proposed European affordable-housing regulation strengthens the legal basis for the policy. The draft EU framework would set conditions under which authorities can restrict short-term rentals in stressed housing markets, and Collboni said it recognizes that tourist accommodation can reduce homes available to residents. The tourist-apartment association Apartur disputes that reading, arguing that any restriction would require strict justification and that the city's blanket ban is disproportionate.
stories.headline: Barcelona reaffirms plan to eliminate 10,000 tourist flats by 2028 after European rules update

stories.body: Catalonia's September 11 Diada will combine institutional events with pro-independence demonstrations in Barcelona, Girona and Amposta under the slogan “I am here. We are here. For the present and the future: Independence.” In Barcelona, two protest columns will leave at 5:14pm from Gran Via at Casanova and Via Laietana by the cathedral, converging at Plaça de Catalunya. The day also includes the traditional floral tribute to Rafael Casanova, concerts at the Festa per la Llibertat and the Generalitat's institutional ceremony at the Teatre Nacional de Catalunya.
stories.headline: Catalonia prepares for Diada demonstrations in Barcelona, Girona and Amposta
